extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, computer scientists, and students writing technical/mathematical papers (CS/Math authors and copy-editing students)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style and copy-editing guidance for mathematical and technical exposition: grammar, semantics, symbols, organization, and proof presentation aimed at improving clarity, concision, and reader focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for clarity, coherence, accuracy, and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing must be clear, coherent, accurate, and concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rosalie's injunction: cut sentences shorter where possible; remove unnecessary words and phrases. Pascal quote: longer drafts often reflect inability to shorten. Examples: replace long constructions with shorter ones; prefer periods to long sentences joined by semicolons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer more questions than you raise
rubrics_metrics.description: A hallmark of good writing is that it answers more questions than it raises; avoid leaving the reader puzzled by vague or incomplete statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t write sentences that prompt immediate follow-up questions (e.g., 'Another solution lies in persuading...' — solution to what? who should persuade?). Make explicit the referents and scopes you implicitly rely on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subject and verb close
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separating subject and verb by many intervening words; long separations make sentences hard to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to move the subject near the verb or split into shorter sentences. Example: change sentences where subject and verb are 'too far apart' or where relative clauses bury the main clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminate needless phrases and fluff
rubrics_metrics.description: Delete superfluous constructions like 'he has heard', 'the reason for ... is that', and similar wordy phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'Dr. Shaffer said one of the most encouraging signs is the fact he has heard one of the largest paper manufacturers...' with 'Dr. Shaffer said one of the largest paper manufacturers...'. Replace 'The reason for removing the spaces from the list is that...' with 'We remove the spaces because...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use semicolons sparingly; prefer periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Semicolons slow the pace and often indicate a sentence should be split; use semicolons only when clauses have a very close relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow William Zinsser's advice: semicolon often conveys '19th-century mustiness'. Use a period if two sentences can convey the same information more clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive repetition of small words
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent repetition of words like 'this', 'they', 'just', or 'then' weakens prose and confuses readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read aloud to spot over-uses; vary wording or restructure sentences to eliminate needless repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conversational idioms and colloquialisms in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Anyway, ...', 'pretty straightforward', or awkward combinations like 'again iterate through' are inappropriate in formal technical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, formal phrasing in papers; reserve conversational idioms for contexts where tone permits them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor subject–verb–object and minimize passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Sticking to SVO style and avoiding passive constructions improves readability and reduces distractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, use active constructions or even imperative/indicative forms ('Multiply each b.z by this factor.' rather than passive or wordy alternatives). Using 'we' to avoid passive is acceptable but often avoidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'noise-phrases' cautiously (e.g., 'in the context of')
rubrics_metrics.description: Delete noise-phrases when they add nothing; but retain them when they help re-establish context for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide by whether the phrase clarifies repetition of the topic; if used early and repeated later it can help orientation, otherwise delete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be venue-aware but prioritize clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Different venues (newspapers vs. scientific journals) may favor different sentence styles, but clear writing is always good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers prioritize simple, direct sentences; mathematical contexts may permit more structured sentences and explicit 'then's to aid parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure pronoun references are explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid constructions with unclear pronoun antecedents (e.g., 'It is unlikely...' without identifying 'it').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to name the referent or restructure the sentence to remove ambiguous pronouns; there is no uniform rewrite rule but alternatives usually exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch placement of 'only'
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of 'only' in a sentence changes meaning drastically; misplaced 'only' is a common error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about intended scope: contrast 'Here we only calculate the position of two vertices' vs 'Here we calculate the position of only two vertices.' Consider all possible positions to ensure correct meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague intensifiers like 'really'
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague words such as 'really' often carry little technical content and should be replaced by precise qualifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'saving the computation for the place where it is really needed' with a concrete criterion (e.g., 'those vertices where the additional work contributes more to the visual quality'). Decide whether modifier makes substantive contribution or is merely colloquial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect domain-specific usages but be aware they can sound odd
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical disciplines sometimes use constructions uncommon in general English (e.g., 'object witness a property'); recognize and accept these when standard in the field, but clarify when ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If usage is common in the field, it may be acceptable; otherwise, consider rephrasing for broader readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words precisely; avoid frequently conflated pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many word pairs are commonly confused (e.g., 'alternately' vs 'alternatively', 'imply' vs 'infer', 'disinterested' vs 'uninterested').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult lists of commonly conflated words and ensure correct meaning is used. Examples and mnemonic contrasts are provided in the notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disambiguate numerals vs words
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'one' could be a numeral or pronoun, prefer the numeral '1' to remove ambiguity where you mean the numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'What are we to do when x is one?' — use '1' when numeral sense intended; prefer 'The only solutions are 2 or 3.' over ambiguous wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize material; avoid distracting the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Two central rules: 'Do organize material' and 'Do not distract the reader.' Organization is crucial and worth most of the writing time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave branches and alternative threads coherently; examine textbooks and well-structured expositions for models. Good organization is recognized when seen; spend time restructuring for flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive about semantic change and usage debates (e.g., 'hopefully')
rubrics_metrics.description: Some word usages evolve (like the sentential use of 'hopefully'); these changes may be acceptable but can distract readers who object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid usages that will distract your audience; use forms that minimize reader annoyance—especially for broad audiences; consider authoritative usage panels and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat grammar as an aid to clarity (cases, who/whom, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar supplies logical structure; respecting cases and grammatical form clarifies thinking and avoids distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nominative/accusative properly ('I don't know who is the President...' not 'whom' in that case). Attention to logical rules of grammar improves exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rigidly enforce archaic rules (e.g., don't ban terminal prepositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules such as 'never end a sentence with a preposition' are reactionary and can force awkward wording; preserve natural phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept prepositions in post-position when natural; don't perform needless gymnastics. However, avoid constructions that result in clumsy or confusing sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place quotation marks logically
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should be placed logically rather than according to arbitrary typographical convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul recommends logical punctuation (placing quotation marks to reflect logical scope). Be consistent and favor reader comprehension over typographic dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid echoing unusual words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not repeat unusual words in unrelated passages since repetition may cause unintended associations or omissions by typists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two uses of the same unusual word are unrelated, substitute synonyms or rephrase to avoid linking them in the reader’s mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' judiciously; consider imperatives and indicatives instead
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'we' to avoid passive voice can add an irrelevant dimension; sometimes imperative or indicative sentences are clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform 'We can now prove...' into concise forms like 'Consequence: A implies B.' or imperatives: 'Replace x by 7 throughout.' Use 'we' sparingly in formal technical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid first-person singular in formal technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person singular can be perceived as immodest or distracting; generally avoid it in formal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer passive, 'we', or impersonal constructions (judiciously) in formal papers; reserve 'I' for contexts where personal voice is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs over proofs by contradiction for exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction are sometimes the easiest when solving a problem, but for exposition prefer direct proofs when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace circuitous contradiction proofs with direct arguments where possible to improve clarity of exposition (example: linear independence proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use punctuation and emphasis sparingly (exclamation points, splitting infinitives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points should be reserved for true exclamations; splitting infinitives and other once-taboo constructs are acceptable when they improve emphasis or readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities differ; avoid gratuitous exclamation points. Splitting infinitives can provide emphasis and avoid awkward rewrites; don't follow proscription blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'that' and 'then' where they aid parsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit 'that' when unnecessary, but retain it in complex sentences where it clarifies structure; include 'then' in mathematical contexts to help fast parsing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance brevity and clarity: 'He said he was going' may be better than 'He said that he was going' in simple cases; in technical sentences, retain 'that' to avoid syntactic ambiguity. Similarly, omit 'then' in simple prose but keep it when the reader is parsing mathematical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincident punctuation conventions are not a problem
rubrics_metrics.description: When punctuation marks coincide (e.g., comma + period) write only the appropriate single mark; coincident punctuation is not indicative of bad construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where two punctuation marks coincide, follow the typographic convention (one mark only). Example: when comma and period collide, write the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer readable typographical forms for math (avoid awkward fraction typesetting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novice typesetters may produce hard-to-read constructions; use conventional readable forms (e.g., slashed fractions or properly set fractions) rather than cramped inline constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mathematical notation is typeset for readability (e.g., use n(n+1)/2 rather than an awkward stacked inline form).
